4947.prule: Reconstructed, weight-sensitive word accent (the script writes no vowels, so every statement is a comparative hypothesis): a long syllable attracts the accent and the final syllable is normally unaccented. Pardee (open text, Arabic-type rule): accent on the third syllable from the end unless a long vowel intervenes, in which case the long-vowel syllable is accented. Tropper (primary, excerpt grade, Akkadian-type rule): the accent falls on the ultima only when it holds a contraction vowel from a triphthong; otherwise it moves forward from the end of the word to the first long syllable; if the word has no long syllable, the first syllable is accented. Both authors hedge ('dürften', 'wahrsch.', 'working hypothesis', 'On the basis of data from the other languages').

4951.prule: Fixed initial: a weak expiratory (dynamic) stress falls on the vowel of the first syllable of the word. tn.translation: Stress in Ulch, as in Nanai or Udihe, is expiratory-musical: a weak expiratory stress falls on the vowel of the first syllable, a tonic (or musical) one on the vowel of the last syllable. The vowel of the first syllable is articulated most distinctly. The vowel of the last syllable, on the contrary, is articulated indistinctly, but with a certain, sometimes barely noticeable, rise in pitch. It is therefore precisely in the last syllable of the word that phonetic processes of reduction … most often occur.

4954.heavy: Weight criterion in (9): (Vː) = heavy (vowel length occurs only in the first syllable). Proposed hierarchy (13): V extra-light (extrametrical) < CV light (single mora) < (C)Vː heavy (double mora), i.e. onset presence counts before nucleus length; codas 'largely irrelevant' except root-final laterals in some approximant-initial bisyllables (fn. 4).
4954.dflt: Penultimate (right-aligned trochee): initial in C-initial bisyllables, second syllable in trisyllables; bisyllables with a short onsetless initial vowel take final stress (degenerate foot on the second syllable).
4954.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the root (right-aligned moraic trochee, rightmost stress rule) in seven of the eight root shapes of Table 3: initial in consonant-initial and long-vowel-initial bisyllables (katha /ˈkat̪a/, uuku /ˈuːku/, ngaani /ˈŋaːni/), second syllable in all trisyllables regardless of onset or vowel length (koloyi /kɔˈlɔji/, ilantyi /iˈlaɲci/, aaliman /ˌaːˈliman/). The one systematic departure (pattern 1, about 9% of roots): bisyllabic roots beginning with a short onsetless vowel take final stress (ikan /iˈkan/), analysed as an unfooted extra-light initial plus a degenerate foot. So in bisyllables both onset presence (ikan vs katha) and initial-vowel length (ikan vs uuku) decide where primary stress falls; in trisyllables neither does, and a long initial vowel there only adds secondary stress. Vowel length occurs only in the first syllable. Stress is morphologically insensitive.
4954.srule: Secondary stress on a long-vowel (heavy) root-initial syllable of trisyllabic roots, which forms its own moraic foot before the penultimate primary (Table 3 patterns 6, 8: aaliman /ˌaːˈliman/, kaarrimpa /ˌkaːˈrimpa/; also iilatha /ˌiːˈlat̪a/, yaantyintyimun /ˌjaːɲˈciɲcimun/); compound-like quadrisyllabic roots take primary stress on the first item and secondary on the second (koorokooro /ˈkɔːɹɔˌkɔɹɔ/, kopupinta /ˈkɔpuˌpinta/). No rhythmic/alternating secondary stress: light-initial trisyllables and increment quadrisyllables carry a single stress (koloyi /kɔˈlɔji/, maytukuntyi /majˈtukuɲci/).

4959.prule: Stress is called 'functional and predictable' but no positional rule for the word as such is stated; every explicit statement ties stress to morpheme identity: inflectional suffixes are either unstressed (feminine -a, §4 p. 455; fem. sg. dir. -a, masc. sg. obl. -e and pl. dir. -e, all glossed '(unstressed)' in the table of §8 p. 456; preterite/imperfect endings; Gandomābādi imperfect -ay) or stressed (fem. sg. obl. -é and pl. obl. -ā́n in the same table, p. 456; sg. obl. -é(y) and pl. dir. -é on nouns in -á, §10 p. 457, whose pl. obl. -iān is printed without an accent; the present personal endings, 'all of which are stressed', p. 462; the perfect's 'stressed e', p. 463; Gandomābādi perfect -áy, p. 464); verbal prefixes be-/mi- are unstressed in preterite, imperfect and present, while in the subjunctive the prefix bé- carries the stress (bé-gen-em vs present mi-gen-ém, p. 462); in the preterite 'the stress is placed on the last syllable of the stem' (p. 463). 4961.prule: One primary (high) stress per noun or verb word; its position is set morphologically, not by syllable count or weight: by default on the first vowel of the root, but lexically specified affixes (e.g. inchoative -aw-, slow-reduplication -aC) take the high stress and reduce the stem to low (or occasionally secondary) stress; after a weak (schwa) root a word-final monoconsonantal grammatical suffix (-m, -c, -n) is included in the stress domain so that stress falls on the schwa between root and suffix rather than on the root schwa (the consonantal suffix itself cannot bear stress); stress falls in different places in the perfective and imperfective aspect forms of one root (Kinkade 1993: 183). Compounds carry one primary stress.
4961.srule: Secondary stress reported, placement not given: Kinkade 1963 (sec. 1.1.2) distinguishes high (primary), secondary and low stress phonemes; 'Compound and reduplicated stems frequently have a high and a secondary stress, but the order in which they occur is variable. Secondary stress is not as common as high stress'; a stem whose affix takes the high stress is 'reduced to low, or occasionally secondary, stress'. No rhythmic or positional rule. Rowicka 2000: 113-114 instead describes Upper Chehalis as a system 'where only primary stress is manifested'.

4962.dq: In this article, we intend to explore precisely one such phenomenon, namely lexical stress in three Portuguese-based creoles, i.e. Guinea-Bissau Kriyol (henceforth K) ... [p. 2]; (15) Heavy syllables attract stress in K iff (a) they constitute the left or right periphery of the phonological word ... [p. 12]; fn. 2: We abstract away, not innocuously probably, from the physical realization of stres…
4962.dloc: Preprint sec. 1 'Introduction' p. 2 ('lexical stress... Guinea-Bissau Kriyol') with fn. 2 (pp. 2-3); sec. 2 p. 12, rule (15) ('periphery of the phonological word'); published pp. 97-109.
4962.heavy: A heavy syllable is one that has a realized coda, and the list of possible codas appears to be the same in K and S and in Portuguese, viz. sonorants and approximants (/l/, /r/, /N/, /I/, /U/) and /s/ [p. 3]; plural /-s/ does not count [p. 11]; for rule (15) the authors add 'left-heavy' syllables made heavy by a branching onset (N + prenasalized consonant), which count only at the left edge of the phonological word, versus 'right-heavy' (coda) syllables, which count only at the right edge [p. 12].
4962.prule: Nouns: stress the penultimate syllable unless the final syllable is heavy, i.e. has a realized coda (/l/, /r/, /N/, glides /I/ /U/, /s/ - but not the plural suffix -s), in which case the final syllable is stressed (plánta, minjér, kabás vs kásas). Verbs: final stress irrespective of syllable structure (plantá, kumé, bambú).
4962.srule: Not mentioned in Andrade & Kihm 2000 (preprint pp. 1-17 read). Kihm & Laks 1989 (instrumental, one Bissau speaker): secondary stresses are optional 'echoes' whose position follows from the main stress -- in nouns/adjectives of three or more syllables a possible but non-regular echo on the initial syllable (àplikasón, pùrgisúzu); in polysyllabic verbs (initial main stress in their analysis) an echo of variable strength on the final syllable. Bull 1989 p. 77 (second-hand via Chapouto 2014 p. 17): trisyllabic final-stressed nouns and numerals of more than three syllables carry a secondary stress on the first syllable.
4962.quote: This suggests a very simple rule, for all intents and purposes identical with that which seems to hold in Portuguese, namely: assign stress to the penultimate syllable, unless the ultimate syllable is heavy, in which case it bears stress. A heavy syllable is one that has a realized coda, and the list of possible codas appears to be the same in K and S and in Portuguese, viz. sonorants and approximants (/l/, /r/, /N/, /I/, /U/) and /s/. [p. 3] ... In K and B, in contrast, the syntactic category of the lexical items is a crucial piece of information: nouns are stressed according to their syllab…
4962.loc: Preprint section 2 'Lexical stress in K, S, and B': pp. 3 (noun rule, examples (1)-(2)), 4-5 (verb rule, example (3); residue lápis), 6-8 (bambú, kumé; N ntíndi vs N pañá), 10-12 (rules (13) and (15), fn. 13 disyllabic-verb restriction, kásas/kabás, sángra); published pp. 97-109.

[p. 5] ... plural /-s/ as opposed to base-internal final /s/ does not make the syllable it attaches to heavy in the relevant sense (compare kásas ‘houses’ and kabás ‘calabash’). [p. 11] ... More …
4962.tone: Andrade & Kihm treat Kriyol as a stress language and abstract away from the phonetic realization (fn. 2, referring to 'Kihm & Laks 1990, L'accent en kriyol, Linx' = Kihm & Laks 1989, De l'accent en kriyol, Linx 20: 89-111, an instrumental study (duration, pitch and intensity measured per syllable, one Bissau speaker) which concludes that Kriyol is a stress language, 'le kriyol est bien une langue à accent': one maximally prominent syllable per accentual unit, with secondary 'echo' stresses in longer words). Chapouto 2014 p. 17 reports Couto 1994 as concluding that a tonal contour is evident in traditional creole, with stress more patent in the lusitanised variety; Bull 1989, Andrade et al. 1992 and Kihm 1994 all treat it as accentual. The Frontiers 2021 creole-prosody survey lists Guinea-Bissau Kriyol as analysed as stress, not tone.

tn.quote: dans un système de type accentuel, une et une seule syllabe par domaine accentuable présente une proéminence absolue. ... De ce point de vue, le kriyol est bien une langue à accent. Toute unité accentuable ... présente une et une seule syllabe maximalement proéminente. ... la proéminence syllabique ne possède pas de corrélats absolus: elle peut se traduire par une augmentation de l'intensité, de la longueur, de la hauteur ou toute combinaison possible de ces facteurs. Il en est ainsi en kriyol.
tn.translation: in an accentual-type system, one and only one syllable per accentual domain shows an absolute prominence. ... From this point of view, Kriyol is indeed an accent language. Every accentual unit ... shows one and only one maximally prominent syllable. ... syllabic prominence has no absolute correlates: it may be expressed by an increase in intensity, length, pitch, or any combination of these factors. So it is in Kriyol.
tn.cite: Kihm, Alain & Bernard Laks. 1989. De l'accent en kriyol. Linx 20: 89-111 (Persée text of pp. 89-111); also checked Andrade & Kihm 2000, Stress in three creoles (preprint), fn. 2, and Chapouto 2014 p. 17.

4965.dq: Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root. [...] These rules work within the root. [...] The "vowel harmony" rule does not apply over morpheme or word boundaries. (p. 111; the data are 'About 230 two-syllable and three-syllable words in frame', p. 110; intonation is treated separately in 4.3.3)
4965.dloc: Section 4.3.1 'Stress', pp. 109-112: opening p. 109 (last paragraph) and p. 110; 'vowel harmony' rule p. 110 (last two paragraphs); stress rule and examples p. 111 (first paragraph, example lists, editor's fn 3); secondary stress p. 111 (last paragraph); reduplication p. 112 (first paragraph) (image PDF)
4965.heavy: Not a syllable-weight criterion. The stress rule as printed is 'Stress is on the first full vowel syllable of the root' (p. 111), but the full/reduced status of a vowel is not a lexical property: the central vowel is 'not... an independent phoneme' (p. 109), 'neither are phonemic' (p. 111), and it is produced by the 'vowel harmony' rule (p. 110) from the relative openness or identity of the two successive vowels. The conditioning of stress is therefore the vowels' relative height/identity: V1 more open than V2 -> V1 stays full and is stressed (['karek], ['atok], ['komuŋ]); V1 more closed than V2, or the two identical -> V1 reduces to [ə] and stress is on the second syllable ([tən'tar], [nə'nol], [kə'lu], [nəm'ba]). The printed wording of the harmony rule and of editor's fn 3 has the open/closed polarity inverted relative to these examples. Residue the source does not derive: /ta.'pon/ [təpo:n] 'to squeeze' (p. 110; a > o yet reduced), 'u could sometimes occur in this less prominent postion' unreduced (p. 110), and word-initial [ə] whose underlying vowel 'is not obvious' (/arpm.a/ [ərpm'a] 'to be', /ə.nu/ [ə'nu] 'female', p. 111). Stress correlates: at least two of louder, longer, less ballistic (slower amplitude decay), non-centralized vowel.
4965.dflt: not applicable (segmental conditioning, not weight). Every root has a stressable full-vowel syllable, since the central vowel 'never occurs in one-syllable words or in word final syllables' (p. 109).
4965.prule: Within the root, stress falls on the first syllable whose vowel is a full (non-central) vowel, and which syllable that is depends on the vowels of the successive syllables, not on syllable weight: as the paper's own example lists show it, when V1 is more open than V2 the first vowel stays full and takes the stress (['karek] 'hen, rooster', ['atok] 'white ant', ['komuŋ] 'a bird', ['wendiŋ] 'junction'); when V1 is more closed than V2 or the two vowels are phonemically identical, V1 is reduced to the non-phonemic central vowel [ə] and stress falls on the second syllable ([tən'tar] 'miserable', [nə'nol] 'mushroom', [kə'lu] 'bottom', [nəm'ba] 'dog', [tə'kor] 'not red'). Stress is cued by at least two of louder, longer, less ballistic (slower amplitude decay), non-central vowel; stress and the central vowel are both non-phonemic. The printed 'vowel harmony' rule (p. 110) and the editor's fn 3 (p. 111) state the open/closed polarity the other way round from the examples; the later Hemmilä & Luoma grammar, as carried by Wood 2012:7, states it the examples' way (V1 more open than V2 -> initial, otherwise final).
4965.srule: In a three-syllable word stressed on its first syllable, the third syllable usually carries a secondary stress (/wa.rim-pen/ [ˈwarimˌpen] 'young person'); in reduplicated words all parts are stressed, the first with primary stress (/naŋ-naŋ/ [ˈnaŋˌnaŋ] 'sing-sing'). The source says nothing about longer words or about trisyllables stressed on the second syllable.

4967.heavy: a sílaba pesada é sempre do tipo [CVC], [CVː] ou [CVV̯]; a sílaba leve é sempre do tipo [CV̆] (p.22) — heavy = closed syllable, long vowel, or diphthong; light = open short-vowel syllable.
4967.dflt: not applicable: the template forbids lexemes without a heavy syllable (*[CV̆ CV̆]); every lexeme has exactly one heavy syllable.
4967.prule: Stress (strong intensity + high pitch) falls on the heavy syllable (CVC, CVː or CVV) of the lexeme; a light CV syllable is unstressed with low pitch. Since every Chapakura lexeme is #(CV)H#, the one heavy syllable is always lexeme-final: monosyllables are stressed, disyllables have final stress. 4968.prule: Main word stress falls on the penultimate syllable in morphologically simple words (quantity-insensitive, counted from the right edge); Hannß repeats this as the language's tendency (p. 3) and lists penultimate stress among the areal features shared with Aymara and Quechua.
